## When someone else is in the room

Lessons 4.1 and 4.2 mostly watched one brain choosing alone—blurting vs checking, pumping a balloon, discounting tomorrow. This lesson adds a second person. Trust, fairness, and cooperation are social. That is why the classic lab games matter: they turn "will you be fair?" into something you can count.

These are classic lab games. "Nash" here just means the cold, self-interested prediction—not what people always do.

Picture three tables in a behavioral lab:

1. **Ultimatum** — someone offers you a split of $10; if you reject, both get nothing.
2. **Trust** — you send money that grows; the other person decides how much to return.
3. **Prisoner's Dilemma** (and its repeated cousins) — cooperate or defect when mutual cooperation beats mutual defection, but temptation to defect is real.

Cold theory says accept any positive crumb, send nothing, and defect. Real people often reject unfair splits, send something, and cooperate—at least at first.[^1][^2][^3]

## Three games in plain clothes

The **Ultimatum Game** asks one player to offer a split of a pot; the other can accept or reject (rejection zeros both payoffs). Cold theory says accept any positive crumb; real people often reject unfair splits.[^1]

The **Trust Game** lets a first mover send money that grows; a second mover decides how much to return.[^2]

The **Prisoner's Dilemma** (and its repeated cousins) asks whether to cooperate or defect when mutual cooperation beats mutual defection but temptation to defect is real.[^3] Axelrod's tournaments already taught that cooperation needs structure, not only good vibes.[^3]

| Game | Cold prediction | Tea / warmth pattern in packs | Alcohol pattern in packs | Anchors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ultimatum | Tiny offers; accept anything above zero | Offers nearer fair **40%–50%** splits | More rejection of unfair offers (≤ about 30%) | Güth et al. (1982); Morewedge et al. (2014) [^1][^4] |
| Prisoner's Dilemma | Both defect | More mutual cooperation | Volatile defection or sloppy play | Axelrod (1984) [^3] |
| Trust Game | Send nothing; return nothing | Higher first sends and more reciprocity | High sends with higher betrayal risk | Berg et al. (1995) [^2] |

Opening trust is not the same as forever trust. That sentence will do more work than any slogan about boardroom tea service.

## Snapshots under alcohol and warmth

| Game | Result | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ultimatum, alcohol ~0.06% BAC (N = 92) | Unfair-offer (≤20%) rejection **82.4%** vs **58.1%** placebo | Morewedge et al. (2014) [^4] |
| Trust Game / fairness, warm ~60°C mug | First-mover investment about **+24.8%** (pack narrative: ~$7.85 vs $6.29 of $10) | Kang et al. (2011) [^5] |
| Iterated Dilemma, warm drink (pack) | Mutual cooperation rounds 1–10: **62.5%** vs **47.2%** control | Inagaki & Eisenberger (2013; pack) [^6] |

Notice the Ultimatum alcohol result carefully: intoxication raised *rejection* of unfair offers. That is costly altruistic punishment—people turning down money to punish unfairness—not "drunk people accept anything." Alcohol myopia and fairness punishment can both be true in the same session.[^4][^8]

Warmth and ritual can lift **opening** trust (about **+15% to +25%** in cited work). If the other side defects in later rounds, cooperation often collapses. Sensory primes influence opening moves; formal structural incentives and payoff matrices dominate equilibrium outcomes over extended interactions (pack verification note).[^3]

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: Ultimatum, Trust, and Dilemma snapshots"}
| Game | Cold prediction | Tea / warmth pattern in packs | Alcohol pattern in packs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ultimatum | Tiny offers; accept anything above zero | Offers nearer fair **40%–50%** splits | More rejection of unfair offers (≤ ~30%) |
| Prisoner's Dilemma | Both defect | More mutual cooperation | Volatile defection or sloppy play |
| Trust Game | Send nothing; return nothing | Higher first sends and more reciprocity | High sends with higher betrayal risk |

Anchors: Güth et al. (1982) Ultimatum;[^1] Berg, Dickhaut & McCabe (1995) Trust Game;[^2] Axelrod (1984) cooperation structure.[^3]

Snapshots:

- Ultimatum, alcohol ~0.06% BAC (N = 92): unfair-offer (≤20%) rejection **82.4%** vs **58.1%** placebo.[^4]
- Trust / fairness, warm ~**60°C** mug: first-mover investment about **+24.8%** (pack narrative of Kang).[^5]
- Iterated Dilemma, warm drink (pack): mutual cooperation rounds 1–10 about **62.5%** vs **47.2%** control.[^6]

Warmth and ritual can lift **opening** trust (~**+15% to +25%** in cited work); if the other side defects later, cooperation often collapses. Incentives still dominate over a long game.[^3]
:::

## Bridge back to Chapter 3 (do not forget the caveats)

People sometimes hope: "Serve tea and the negotiation becomes win–win forever." Opening trust is real in cited work; forever cooperation is not.

Ritual can also blunt the brain's error-alarm and lower anxiety ([3.4 Ritual stress](../module-03/04-ritual-stress.qmd))—discussed in the packs alongside fewer hyper-aggressive rejections of unfair offers. Calmer bodies can mean less hair-trigger bargaining—not automatic fairness forever.

And remember Chapter 3's replication caution: warmth effects on generosity are smaller and less reliable than early headlines suggested.[^7] Lynott et al. (2014) failed to replicate Williams & Bargh's gift-choice Study 2 at N = 861. Keep that in view when someone sells "serve tea, win the deal."

::: {.callout-caution title="Equilibrium vs priming"}
Thermal and beverage-ritual priming can raise initial trust allocations in cited designs. That cooperative bias often degrades in multi-round games if the counterpart defects. Primes nudge opening moves; payoffs dominate over a long game.[^3][^5]
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Click for more detail: how this lesson uses Chapter 3 without overclaiming"}
- **Warm mug → Trust send** ([3.3](../module-03/03-warmth-trust.qmd) → this lesson): useful as a bridge and as a methods warning for [4.4](04-study-protocols.qmd).
- **Ritual → calmer ERN / lower anxiety** ([3.4](../module-03/04-ritual-stress.qmd)): may reduce hair-trigger Ultimatum rejections in the packs' qualitative framing—not a fairness guarantee.
- **Brooks (2016)**: still **not** evidence after the 2024 retraction.
- **Lynott (2014)**: still the check on "warmth always makes people generous."[^7]
:::

If headlines about drinks and decisions feel loud, the next section is the quiet machinery behind careful studies.


## Play the Ultimatum in your head

Someone offers you $2 of $10. If you accept, you get $2 and they keep $8. If you reject, both get $0. Cold theory says take the $2. Many people reject. Unfairness has a price people are willing to pay.[^1]

Now raise alcohol to ~**0.06%** BAC. In Morewedge et al.'s design (N = 92), rejection of offers ≤20% jumped from **58.1%** to **82.4%**.[^4] Intoxication did not make people "chill about fairness." It made costly punishment *more* likely—emotional reactivity with a price tag.

That surprises beginners who expect alcohol to make everyone say yes. Alcohol myopia narrows attention to vivid cues; unfairness can be a vivid cue.[^8]

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: Trust Game arithmetic (Kang pack narrative)"}
Endowment $10. Warm ~60°C mug vs cold pad.

Pack narrative of Kang et al.: first-mover sends average about **$7.85** (warm) vs **$6.29** (cold)—roughly **+24.8%**.[^5]

Read it as an **opening allocation nudge** under thermal priming—not as "tea creates trustworthy partners forever." If player two defects in later rounds, the cooperative glow often fades (pack equilibrium note).
:::

## Cooperation needs a structure, not only a kettle

Axelrod's tournaments showed that strategies like reciprocity can thrive when games repeat and feedback is clear—structure enables cooperation.[^3] A warm drink may help early coordination (pack Dilemma snapshot: **62.5%** vs **47.2%** mutual cooperation in early rounds).[^6] It does not rewrite the payoff matrix.

So when someone says "serve tea and the boardroom becomes win–win," translate: *maybe a better opening*; *not a new game theory*.



## Ritual calm and unfair offers (qualitative bridge)

The packs link Chapter 3's ritual/ERN story to bargaining: if scripted action blunts the error-alarm and lowers somatic anxiety, people may be less hair-trigger about rejecting mid-unfair offers. That is a **qualitative bridge**, not a new Ultimatum experiment unique to tea.

Keep the chain honest:

1. Ritual can reduce anxiety / blunt ERN in cited work ([3.4](../module-03/04-ritual-stress.qmd)).
2. Anxiety and emotional reactivity can raise costly punishment (alcohol Ultimatum).[^4]
3. Therefore calmer bodies *might* mean fewer hyper-aggressive rejections—without guaranteeing fair offers or forever cooperation.

Brooks (2016) still cannot be used to decorate step 1.
